title: The Day of Fracture
teaser: Every survivor remembers where they stood when the sky cracked.
lore:
Every survivor remembers where they stood when the sky cracked.

It began as a sound — not thunder, the old archivists insist, but a chord, as if the whole Dominion were a string drawn too tight and finally plucked. The Spire of Accord, where the five provinces had kept their treaties and their treasures for nine hundred years, lit from within like a lantern. Then the light went wrong.

The ground did not shake. It separated. Roads ended in sky. Rivers poured upward into nothing and returned as snow three provinces away. When the chord faded, the Dominion was no longer one land but a scatter of shards drifting on a sea of pale mist, each carrying a piece of the old world and none carrying the whole truth.

The Spire itself was simply gone. In its place hung the Fracture: a seam of white fire stitched across the heavens, visible from every shard, burning to this day.

What the chord was, who struck it, and why the arcane wards of the Spire — wards that had never once failed — sang along instead of holding fast: these are the questions this Chronicle exists to answer. The first clue lies with the arcanists who survived. Their hands, every one, were burned in the same spiral pattern.

title: The Shattered Archive
teaser: The Archive answered every question but one — and split rather than answer it.
lore:
Before the Fracture, the Shattered Archive was simply the Archive: a mountain hollowed into shelves, staffed by an order sworn to record everything and judge nothing.

When the shards settled, scavengers found the Archive split clean down its centre, as if a blade had passed through forty miles of stone. Books on the western face ended mid-sentence; their other halves drifted on a shard eleven days' sail away. The archivists who survived did something unprecedented: they stopped recording, and started searching their own stacks.

What they sought was the Accord Ledger — the sealed record of what the five provinces had stored in the Spire's deepest vault. The Ledger's shelf was found empty. Not looted: empty, with dust undisturbed, as though the book had been removed years before the Fracture and the absence politely catalogued by no one.

One marginal note survives, in the hand of Chief Archivist Veyle, dated thirty days before the sky cracked: 'The fifth province has asked again about the vault. I have told them again that what sleeps under the Accord is not ours to wake. They have stopped asking. That worries me more.'

Veyle's trail leads to the iron province — to the Citadel that armed itself, quietly, in the final month of the old world.

title: The Iron Testament
teaser: The Citadel forged for a war it never declared — against an enemy it never named.
lore:
The Iron Citadel survived the Fracture better than any other power, and that fact alone has fed a generation of accusations.

Its foundries were running at war tempo a full month before the sky cracked. Conscription rolls, recovered from a drowned customs-shard, show the Citadel recalling every soldier it had ever lent out — quietly, in small groups, under orders marked TESTAMENT. No war was declared. No enemy was named.

The Testament orders themselves were thought lost until a salvage crew cut open a strongroom fused shut by Fracture-heat. Inside: a single iron tablet, addressed to the Citadel's marshals, seven words long.

'It is waking early. Hold the line.'

Not an invasion. Not a rival province. It. The Citadel knew what slept beneath the Spire of Accord, knew it was stirring, and chose to arm rather than warn. Whether that was treachery or triage divides the shards to this day — because when the chord finally sounded, the Citadel's legions were the only force standing close enough to the Spire to see what came out.

Of the First Legion, nine thousand strong, the mist returned exactly one survivor. She has never spoken. She only draws: page after page of the same spiral that scarred the arcanists' hands.

reward.name: Iron Testament Tablet
reward.desc: A replica of the Citadel's seven-word order.
reward.lore: It is waking early. Hold the line.

title: The Hollow Choir
teaser: The dead of the Fracture did not all stay where they fell.
lore:
The dead of the Fracture did not all stay where they fell.

On the ash-shards, where the burning seam hangs lowest in the sky, the fallen began to walk within a season. Not as mindless husks — that was the horror of it. They walk with purpose, always toward the Fracture, gathering at the broken edges of their shards and standing in silent congregations a thousand strong, faces turned upward. Travellers call them the Hollow Choir.

They do not attack unless turned away from the seam. They do not rot past a certain point, as if held. And on the longest night of each year, every congregation on every shard kneels at the same instant — an act of coordination no living census could match.

A heretic scholar named Ostrava lived among a congregation for a year, the only living soul they tolerated. Her final dispatch, sent by gull before her shard drifted into the deep mist, reads: 'They are not worshipping it. I was wrong, we were all wrong. They are guarding it. Something on our side of the seam frightens the dead more than whatever waits on the other side, and I have begun to dream of spirals.'

No shard has sighted Ostrava's congregation since.

title: The Fifth Province
teaser: Four provinces signed the Accord in ink. The fifth signed in something else.
lore:
Children on every shard can name the four provinces: forest, iron, ash, and frost. The treaties stored in the Spire of Accord, though, were always signed five times.

The fifth signature appears on no map and belongs to no banner. In the recovered treaty fragments it is not written but woven — a thread of something that is not ink and not metal, stitched through the parchment in a tight, familiar spiral. Archivist Veyle's private cipher, cracked at last this season, names the fifth signatory only as the Custodian, and records the terms of its accord in one chilling line: 'The Custodian keeps the vault, and the vault keeps the Custodian.'

The old Dominion, it seems, was never a union of equals. It was a perimeter. Four provinces arranged around a fifth thing, feeding the Spire's wards for nine hundred years, calling the arrangement peace.

Veyle's cipher ends with an itinerary: she was bound for the Spire itself, carrying the missing Accord Ledger, twenty-two days before the Fracture. Her last line: 'If the Custodian's terms were broken, it was not the Custodian who broke them. I go to learn which of us did. If the sky should crack before I return, look for my hand in the light.'

The deep-mist salvagers swear the seam above the old Spire-site flickers, some nights, in the shape of a writing hand.

title: The Custodian's Bargain
teaser: The Fracture was not an attack. It was an expiry.
lore:
Assemble the pieces and the shape of the truth is finally visible.

Nine hundred years ago, something vast was bound beneath the Spire of Accord — not defeated, bound, by a bargain. The Custodian would sleep, and the five-fold Accord would feed its wards; the provinces got an age of peace, and the Custodian got an age of dreaming. Every treaty, every tithe, every arcane circuit in the Dominion was, knowingly or not, a clause in that contract.

Then the fifth province stopped asking about the vault — because someone had given them an answer. The Accord Ledger left the Archive in silence. The Citadel armed for a holder's war it could not win. The wards, starved or sabotaged, sang along with the chord instead of holding it. The bargain expired, and the Dominion was the collateral.

But here is what the Hollow Choir and the burned spiral hands and Veyle's flickering signature in the seam all agree on: the Custodian has not yet left. The Fracture is not a wound — it is a door, held ajar from the inside, and everything that walks or fights or rebuilds on the shards is being watched through it with an interest the old treaties never described.

The Chronicle's first season closes with the question that will open the next: the Custodian kept its half of the bargain for nine hundred years. Now it is awake, unbound, and patient — and somewhere in the mist, on a shard no map carries, the Accord Ledger is waiting to tell someone the terms of the next one.

reward.name: Fracture Lens
reward.desc: A shard of Spire-glass. Hold it to the seam and the light bends into a spiral.
reward.lore: Look for my hand in the light. — Chief Archivist Veyle

title: The Archive's Last Silence
teaser: The order swore to record everything and judge nothing. Then it learned something it could not simply file.
lore:
For nine hundred years the Archive's order kept one oath: record everything, judge nothing. They kept it through border wars they could have ended with a single sentence. They kept it through the Fracture itself, when the mountain split down its centre and half their shelves went sailing off into the mist with the words still on them.

They broke it on an ordinary morning, in a reading room with the shutters closed.

What Veyle's cracked cipher had finally handed them was not a rumour. It was a set of terms — the shape of a bargain struck beneath the Spire of Accord, the date of its expiry, and the plain fact that the thing which had kept its half of it for nine centuries is keeping nothing now. To write that down and say nothing would be, by the order's own reckoning, a species of lie their oath had never thought to forbid. To say it aloud would put the same sentence into the mouth of every frightened shard-town from the Iron Citadel to the last frost-outpost: it is awake, and it is watching.

The order argued for four days. The transcript runs to two hundred pages and contains, by one deputy's exhausted count, every position a living person has ever held on whether the truth is a gift or a weapon. It ends without a vote — because on the fifth morning they found the question had already left the building. Someone had begun copying pages. Nobody has ever admitted to it, and the order has never once gone looking, which the shards have taken as an answer of its own.

What happens next was never really the Archive's to decide. It is being decided right now, in a hundred reading rooms and guardhouses and kitchens, by people who have just learned that the thing beneath the world is not a story told to children. You are one of them.

decision.prompt: The pages are already moving and cannot be called back. A deputy archivist — young, inked to the elbow, entirely out of her depth — asks what you would have them do now.

options.label: Say nothing more
options.consequence: Let the copied pages be the whole of it. A frightened Dominion is a loud one, and whatever watches through the seam has had nine hundred years to learn what our noise means.

options.label: Publish it properly
options.consequence: Half-copied pages breed worse rumours than the truth ever could. You argue for the full record, openly — every province, every shard, the terms set out plainly, so that whatever comes next is settled by people who know what they are settling with.

options.label: Find the Ledger first
options.consequence: Terms are worth nothing without the contract they came from. You leave the archivists to their argument and start asking, quietly, who last saw the Accord Ledger — and whether the shard it went down with is still on anybody's chart.

title: The First Vigil
teaser: The Custodian is awake. The Dominion must answer for the first time in nine hundred years.
lore:
News does not travel fast across the shards, but this news did not need to. Within a week of the Archive's proclamation — that something ancient slept beneath the old Spire, and sleeps no longer — every square from the Iron Citadel to the last frost-outpost had heard some version of the same sentence: it is awake, and it is watching.

The Hollow Choir's kneeling nights have grown longer. In three border towns the seam itself has begun to flicker at dusk, the old spiral shape rising and dissolving in the white fire like something practicing a signature. The Archive has stopped calling it the Fracture in its new bulletins. They call it, carefully, the door.

Nobody in power has decided what to do about a door. So the deciding has fallen, as it always does in the end, to the shard-folk who have to live nearest it — travellers, soldiers, merchants, the newly Worldmended who thought the hard part was over. Three answers have taken root. Keep the vigil the Choir already keeps, and give the Custodian nothing further to notice. Send envoys, as the old Accord did, and try to strike honest terms before someone strikes dishonest ones. Or go to the door itself, before the Court or the Citadel or worse gets there first, and take the answer directly.

None of the three is wrong. All of them are being tried, in different border towns, by different people, right now. Yours is one more voice added to an argument nine hundred years old.

decision.prompt: A town crier reads the Archive's bulletin aloud, then asks the crowd — asks you — the only question that matters: how do you answer the door?

options.label: Keep the vigil
options.consequence: You say nothing to the door, and everything to the people already watching it. If it wants a reply, let it wait as long as it made others wait.

options.label: Send an envoy
options.consequence: You start drafting terms nobody asked you to draft. If the old Accord could be negotiated once, in ink and nine hundred years of peace, it can be negotiated again — better this time, with everyone's name on it.

options.label: Go to the door
options.consequence: Someone has to go first, and you would rather it be someone who chooses to. You start walking toward the last place any map marks the Spire.

title: The Scattered Answer
teaser: Three answers went out to the door. The door has not yet decided which one it heard.
lore:
Three answers went out from the border towns, as the crier promised, and for a season the Dominion held its breath waiting to see which the door would answer back. It did not have to wait long to learn the truth of it: the door did not answer any of them. It listened to all three at once, and the listening itself began to show.

In the vigil-towns, where the Hollow Choir already kept its silent congregations, watchers report the seam growing calmer wherever a crowd gathers to simply stand and hold the line — the spiral dims, some nights, to little more than a thread. In the towns that sent envoys, letters addressed to nothing more specific than 'the Custodian, care of the Fracture' have begun arriving back unopened, their wax seals broken and resealed in a spiral no living hand pressed there. And of the three scouting parties that set out for the last charted approach to the old Spire-site, only one courier has returned — alone, unhurt, carrying no message, unable or unwilling to say what became of the other two.

Archivist deputies, cataloguing the reports as fast as they arrive, have started calling it the Split Season. Not because the Dominion disagrees — it always has — but because for the first time the disagreement is being answered back, town by town, in three different dialects of silence. Chief Deputy Sorne, who inherited Veyle's desk and none of her certainty, put it plainly in the latest bulletin: 'We assumed a door either opens or it doesn't. Nobody accounted for one that simply waits to see if we can agree on a knock.'

The Iron Citadel, characteristically, has stopped waiting on anyone else's answer. Marshal Coric Vane — the officer who lost the First Legion's sister company and has spent six years since insisting the Testament orders were triage, not treachery — has begun quietly re-arming the same recall lists that armed the Citadel before the Fracture. Not for war, she insists to anyone who'll listen at the garrison gates; for whichever answer the Dominion finally settles on, so that it isn't unescorted when it arrives. Her critics call it the same mistake twice. Her few allies call it the only lesson the Citadel actually learned.

{align:vigil}You have kept your own vigil since the pages first went round, quiet and unclaimed, and the reports from the calm-seamed towns land like confirmation: whatever the Custodian wants, it is not being given anything by your silence, and that has always been the point.{/align}{align:accord}Your letters have gone out through three separate couriers now, and come back unopened like everyone else's, and still you keep drafting the next one — because a door that resealed a letter instead of burning it has, in its own patient way, admitted it can be written to.{/align}{align:unbinding}You have already turned your steps toward the last charted approach, and the single returned courier's silence tells you less than the two who didn't come back at all — somebody has to learn what they saw, and it will not be learned from a border town.{/align}{align:default}You have not yet chosen a side of this argument, and watching the three dialects of silence arrive from three directions, you are beginning to suspect that not choosing is its own kind of answer — just not one you especially like.{/align}

Marshal Vane's recall notices reach your town on the same courier run as Sorne's bulletin, and a Citadel sergeant reads both aloud from the same crate, in the same flat voice, as though the difference between a scholar's caution and a soldier's readiness were smaller than either institution would admit. When she's done, she looks up, and asks the crowd — asks you — the only question the season has actually been building toward: not which answer is right, but which one you are willing to carry the rest of the way.

decision.prompt: The sergeant is asking on Marshal Vane's behalf, but the choice is entirely your own — how do you carry the season's answer forward?

options.label: Join the calm-seamed watch
options.consequence: You go to stand with the vigil-towns properly this time — not waiting alone, but adding your silence to a crowd's, and trusting that a door which quiets around patience is telling the truth about what it wants.

options.label: Carry a letter yourself
options.consequence: You take the next letter out of Sorne's desk before it can be entrusted to another courier who might not return, and set out to deliver it by hand — because if the door is going to reseal something, you would rather it reseal a promise you made in person.

options.label: Ride out with Vane's escort
options.consequence: You volunteer for the Marshal's re-armed recall lists, not to start a fight but to finish a reconnaissance two couriers didn't survive — if the Dominion is going to answer the door directly, someone competent should be standing nearby when it does.
